candidates.title: Negative-differential-resistance chips as beyond-Boolean compute substrate
candidates.shift: A physics review proposes NDR-based transistors as an alternative to conventional monotonic-transport computing, potentially changing chip architecture assumptions.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative and very early-lab-stage, but if it matures it could reshape data-centre chip demand/power profiles — worth flagging against the open 'compute?' hunt zone even though it's off-map today.
candidates.evidence: Review paper describing NDR device physics and 'functionally compressed computing' concept.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of a foundational compute-hardware shift (from monotonic transistor logic to non-monotonic transport) that, if commercialized, could alter power/cooling demands of compute infrastructure embedded in stores and fulfilment centres.
candidates.author: Ying Luo, Weixiao Sun, Yongbiao Zhai et al.

candidates.title: Itinerant off-grid bathhouse as mobile retail/experience unit
candidates.shift: A converted canal boat becomes a fully off-grid bathhouse that relocates every two weeks, combining sauna, plunge pools and a bar as a moving micro-venue.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: reframes 'store' as a temporary, utility-independent, migratory experience node — a genuinely strange precedent for how retail/hospitality could occupy marginal urban infrastructure (waterways) without fixed real estate or grid connection.
candidates.evidence: Badweather collective's Soak bathhouse, off-grid, moves along London waterways every two weeks.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of fixed retail/hospitality space giving way to mobile, off-grid, transient occupancy models; if this scales it challenges assumptions that experience venues need permanent utility-connected real estate.
candidates.author: Amina Amber

candidates.title: Brand deadstock reborn as collectible furniture
candidates.shift: A designer converts Vivienne Westwood textile deadstock into sculptural, collectible furniture pieces, treating fashion waste as a materials stream for interiors.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: a small single instance, but points to a possible absence — no established supply chain or category yet for retailer deadstock-to-furniture conversion; could matter for circularity reporting and store fixtures sourcing.
candidates.evidence: Oliver Stiff's furniture line built from Vivienne Westwood deadstock materials, RCA graduate project.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of circular-economy logic moving from apparel resale into secondary material categories (furniture); if formalized, retailers could need deadstock-diversion contracts and new SKUs for fixtures/interiors made from their own waste.
candidates.author: Rachael Gilby

candidates.title: Clothing thermal properties as urban heat-comfort lever
candidates.shift: Simulation study compares how fabric radiative properties affect outdoor thermal comfort across Chinese cities, treating clothing as a variable in urban heat management alongside built form.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative and stretchy for retail real estate, but suggests a future where store frontage, awnings, and even staff uniforms could be assessed jointly with pedestrian thermal comfort metrics as heat events intensify.
candidates.evidence: Simulation of three fabric types' solar reflectivity/emissivity effects on MRT and PET comfort indices in Chinese cities.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of heat-adaptation research expanding from built form (shade, materials) to human-worn materials; if adopted, could inform storefront/streetscape heat-comfort design codes in hot climates.
candidates.author: Chi Feng, Ran Cheng, Siqi Hou et al.

candidates.title: Consolidating scattered public services into one civic hub
candidates.shift: A French public-services center unifies previously separate municipal facilities into a single bridging building serving two districts.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: mirrors retail's own move toward multi-service, community-hub formats — worth watching as a parallel model of consolidation that could compete with or inform mixed-use retail redevelopment.
candidates.evidence: HEMAA Architectes' Jacques Prévert Public Services Center in Évry-Courcouronnes bridges two districts under one roof.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of civic infrastructure consolidation (from dispersed single-service buildings to unified multi-service hubs) that parallels retail's shift toward community/service-anchored formats; could inform how vacant big-box space gets repurposed for public services.
candidates.author: Andreas Luco

candidates.title: Municipality-led open design contest for a new sustainable district
candidates.shift: Madrid region and Leganés launch a public urban-design competition for a new district framed explicitly around sustainability and innovation from the outset.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative and early-stage (just a call for proposals), but signals a policy-first, competition-driven model for greenfield district design that could set retail/mixed-use siting terms before any retailer is involved.
candidates.evidence: Open call urban design contest for 'Puerta de Madrid' district issued by Community of Madrid and Leganés City Council.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of top-down, sustainability-mandated district design preceding tenant/retail decisions; if widespread, retailers would need to respond to pre-set sustainability criteria rather than negotiate them site-by-site.
candidates.author: Rene Submissions

candidates.title: Autonomous robot performing venipuncture without a clinician
candidates.shift: A commercial robot uses near-infrared imaging and ultrasound to locate veins and autonomously draw blood, replacing a phlebotomist's task end-to-end.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: if this scales into retail health clinics (pharmacy/grocery minute-clinics), it changes staffing models, footprint needs (robot bay vs exam room), and liability/insurance questions for in-store healthcare.
candidates.evidence: Vitestro's Aletta robot autonomously performs vein-finding and blood draw via NIR light, ultrasound probe and alcohol prep, described in operational detail.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of physical-AI automating a licensed clinical task; if adopted in retail health settings it shifts labor requirements from clinicians to technicians/attendants and changes in-store clinic floorplans and insurance liability structures.
candidates.author: Elie Dolgin

candidates.title: Greenhouse climate logic migrating into ordinary housing
candidates.shift: Residential design increasingly borrows greenhouse principles — enclosure-controlled sunlight, heat and ventilation — not for plants but for everyday living comfort.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative reframing: if greenhouse-style passive climate control becomes a mainstream domestic design language, it could migrate into retail atria/entryways as a low-energy climate strategy, a genuine reframing of 'store as controlled microclimate'.
candidates.evidence: Feature describes housing projects applying greenhouse enclosure principles (sunlight, heat, ventilation control) to domestic space design.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of a building-science concept (greenhouse enclosure) migrating from a specialized typology into mainstream housing and potentially into commercial atria as passive climate strategy, driven by energy cost and comfort pressures.
candidates.author: Daniela Andino

candidates.title: Underground hydrogen deposits as an untapped energy source
candidates.shift: Exploration efforts are actively searching for naturally occurring underground hydrogen gas reserves as a potential new energy resource.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative and early, but if underground 'white/gold' hydrogen proves extractable at scale it could reshape regional energy-grid mix and on-site power/backup options for large retail and logistics real estate.
candidates.evidence: Newsletter reports a flurry of exploration efforts searching for underground hydrogen gas stores as a potential energy source.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of a new primary-energy source (geologic hydrogen) emerging outside conventional grid/fossil supply chains; if viable, it could change regional utility planning and on-site power resilience strategy for large-footprint retail sites.
candidates.author: Thomas Macaulay

candidates.title: Digital material passports lack a standard taxonomy — for now
candidates.shift: Circular-construction regulation increasingly requires 'digital passports' for buildings/materials, but there is still no standardized, hierarchical data schema to make them interoperable.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative absence signal: the category (material passport) is being mandated before the data standard exists — a genuine gap retailers/developers will need addressed for compliance, resale value, and insurance of building components.
candidates.evidence: Paper proposes semantic topic modelling to build a computational taxonomy for digital building passports, citing lack of standardised data requirements as the current constraint.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of regulation outrunning infrastructure: circular-economy mandates for material passports exist before a common data standard does, an absence that will force retailers/developers to adopt ad hoc systems until standardization arrives.
candidates.author: Silvia Vangelova, Kasimir Forth, Jakob Beetz et al.

candidates.title: International stocktake exposes uneven heat-action-plan readiness
candidates.shift: A cross-country assessment of urban Heat Action Plans finds wide variation in how cities prepare for and manage extreme heat, ahead of what is otherwise a well-covered climate-adaptation trend.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: while HAPs themselves are already a named trend, the finding of uneven, non-standardized implementation is the sharper edge — retail operators in under-prepared cities may face sudden heat-driven operational/liability exposure with no local playbook.
candidates.evidence: International assessment comparing Heat Action Plans across cities worldwide, evaluating preparedness gaps.
candidates.initial_analysis: Already a named trend (heat action plans) but the cross-city comparison reveals an absence of consistent standards — useful for judging which regions will force store-operating-hour, cooling, or insurance changes first.
candidates.author: Saeideh Sobhaninia, Sara Meerow, Ladd Keith et al.

candidates.title: Cost-modelling tools for alternative walling systems, tested in Cameroon
candidates.shift: A BIM-based 5D cost-estimation workflow for alternative (non-standard) walling systems is piloted on a real mixed-use building project in Yaoundé, addressing chronic construction cost overruns.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: peripheral-geography example of quantitative rigor being applied to material substitution decisions in construction — could set a replicable costing standard for markets (Africa, Southeast Asia) building mixed-use retail with alternative materials.
candidates.evidence: Model-based estimating workflow applied to a real, not-yet-started four-storey mixed-use building in Yaoundé, Cameroon, targeting quantity/cost overrun problems.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of BIM-driven cost-estimation rigor emerging from a peripheral-geography project rather than a Western flagship — if the workflow proves reliable it could become an exportable standard for cost-controlled mixed-use construction in emerging retail markets.
candidates.author: Fonbeyin Henry Abanda, Abigaïl Kouoh’a Bebey Emmanuella, Martial Nde et al.

candidates.title: Quantifying the lifecycle cost gap in 3D-printed buildings
candidates.shift: A parametric BIM framework attempts to close the evidence gap on long-term energy and life-cycle cost performance of 3D-printed building envelopes, an area previously assessed mostly on speed/waste-reduction claims.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: 3D-printed construction has been hyped mainly for build speed; this signals the harder second-order question — whether printed envelopes actually perform over decades — which matters directly for retailers considering printed-store construction.
candidates.evidence: Study addresses limited quantitative evidence linking envelope design decisions to long-term energy/economic performance in 3D-printed buildings.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of a construction-tech hype cycle (3D printing) maturing into harder performance questions (lifecycle energy/cost) that will determine whether printed store shells are viable long-term real-estate assets rather than novelty builds.
candidates.author: Abdullah Al Masri, Madhar Haddad, Rodrigo Pierott et al.

candidates.title: Data-analytics gap in last-mile delivery treated as urban infrastructure problem
candidates.shift: A scoping review frames last-mile delivery's inefficiency and environmental cost as fundamentally a data-analytics adoption problem in cities, not just a logistics one.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: touches the open 'delivery format?' hunt zone directly — the absence isn't delivery vehicles or hubs, it's standardized urban data infrastructure to coordinate them, which stores/fulfilment nodes will need to plug into.
candidates.evidence: Scoping review synthesizing studies on how data analytics could address last-mile delivery's cost, efficiency and environmental challenges in urban areas.
candidates.initial_analysis: Already a well-covered problem (last-mile cost/inefficiency) but reframed here as a data-infrastructure absence rather than a fleet/vehicle problem — relevant to how stores design curbside and micro-fulfilment data integration.
candidates.author: Shealtiel Paul Gurrapu, Olivia McDermott, Micheal Sony et al.

candidates.title: Stone exoskeleton replaces steel and concrete in a London high-rise
candidates.shift: A ten-storey apartment building is held up by a load-bearing volcanic-stone exoskeleton instead of conventional concrete/steel structure, claimed as a world-first at this height.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative but concrete: a named structural-engineering first that could shift embodied-carbon calculus for mid-rise retail/mixed-use construction, though code/insurance acceptance for stone-as-structure at scale is untested.
candidates.evidence: Groupwork and Webb Yates' Petra Heights in north London uses roughly a thousand tons of volcanic rock as structural exoskeleton across three blocks (6-10 storeys).
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of a materials substitution (stone-as-structure) challenging the default concrete/steel construction stack; if codes and insurers accept it, it could become an embodied-carbon-reduction option for mid-rise retail/mixed-use buildings.
candidates.author: Jennifer Hahn

candidates.title: Disused nightclub/retail building reborn as public library
candidates.shift: A former nightclub, car park and retail structure is adaptively reused into a public library, wrapping the existing concrete shell in a new material skin rather than demolishing it.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative single instance, but a clean second-order example of retail/leisure real estate obsolescence flowing directly into civic reuse — worth watching as a template for what happens to vacated big-format retail stock.
candidates.evidence: Hudson Architects converted a disused nightclub/retail/car-park structure in King's Lynn, Norfolk into a public library using a cement-shingle skin over the existing concrete structure.
candidates.initial_analysis: Example of vacated commercial/retail real estate being converted to civic use rather than left dark or demolished; if this becomes routine, it changes how landlords, insurers and municipalities value obsolete retail shells.
candidates.author: Jon Astbury

candidates.title: Design sector overtakes retail as UK's largest economic contributor
candidates.shift: A national report finds Britain's design industry has grown 40% and now outweighs retail's contribution to GDP, reframing the relative economic weight of retail versus creative/design services.
candidates.ai_read: Tentative: a named, reported statistic (likely Trend/Context) but its implication is sharper — retail's shrinking share of economic centrality could accelerate landlords repositioning retail real estate toward design/creative-sector tenancy.
candidates.evidence: Design Council report: UK design industry grew 40%, contributing £136.7 billion and now generating more per £20 of national output than retail.
candidates.initial_analysis: Already-reported statistic (included for judgment, likely Context) whose second-order implication — retail losing relative economic centrality to design/creative services — could reshape which tenant classes anchor future retail real estate.
candidates.author: Jane Englefield
